transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-30 16:00 PDT | Duration 54m | Redwood: Maya Lin (AE), Jordan Park (SE) | Customer: Priya Desai (CTO), Ethan Cole (Head of Platform), Lina Gomez (SRE)

Summary: quick discovery focused on unit economics and deploy-mode tradeoffs. Opalshore has strict budget ceilings for pilot and unclear residency needs for PII workflows. Team requested hosted pricing, dedicated reserved options, and a short pilot to validate latency/cost.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching and KV cache impact, hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs, pilot scope and success criteria, security/compliance questions (SOC2, KMS, SSO).

Transcript: 
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick plan — 45-ish minutes to run through your workloads, budget, and then Jordan will do a short latency/cost sketch. is that good?
[00:12] Priya (Opalshore CTO): yeah that works, thanks. we — um — we want to understand where hosted stops being cost-effective and when dedicated or a private deployment makes sense. we have a finance constraint of roughly $15k/month for the pilot.
[00:27] Jordan (Redwood SE): cool. and what's the volume shape — bursty? steady? average request token sizes?
[00:34] Ethan (Head of Platform): mostly bursty during end-of-day routing and a steady trickle during daytime. typical prompt + completion is ~350 tokens, sometimes up to 1.2k for long lookups.
[00:45] Lina (SRE): also want to call out we have a strict egress cap on our cloud account; outbound bandwidth is a gating factor if we go hosted.
[00:56] Maya: perfect, that's helpful. on the per-token side, hosted is simplest — pay-as-you-go. dedicated gives a lower per-token if you commit capacity but requires reservation. private (VPC/on-prem) has higher fixed cost but keeps data in your network and can satisfy KMS/HSM needs.
[01:18] Priya: how big is the delta typically? can you give a back-of-envelope comparing hosted to dedicated for our scale?
[01:25] Jordan: yes — very roughly for a 2M token/month pilot, hosted might be X cents/token — sorry, let me be specific — if you use a 7B-ish open model variant, hosted list price is ~0.12c per 1k tokens; that nets out to about $240 per month at 2M tokens, but that number is very model-dependent and also depends on streaming vs non-streaming and request/response size. for higher-capacity production we see burning less per token via batching and quantized dedicated instances.
[02:05] Ethan: those numbers feel low compared to our budget floor — where's the rest of the cost? is the math off?
[02:12] Jordan: right sorry — i was describing compute-only baseline. there are operational costs — reserved GPUs for dedicated, amortized infra, SRE time, and also caching patterns. you can drop per-token compute by aggressive batching and KV cache reuse. for example, with good prefix caching for synchronous reranking or chat context reuse you can reduce call tokens by 20-60%.
[02:40] Priya: can you explain prefix/KV caching? we saw that phrase in the doc but not sure how it maps to our flows.
[02:47] Jordan: sure — imagine many requests share the same system prompts or instruction prefixes. Redwood can cache key-value attention states for those prefixes. on subsequent calls you don't re-compute that portion — so effective tokens processed by GPU are lower. that saves compute and costs; caching is most effective when you have repeated templates.
[03:10] Lina: is that automatic or something we tune? any risk in cache poisoning or stale data?
[03:16] Jordan: it's configurable — default safe TTLs and controls for invalidation. for PII-sensitive inputs you'd avoid caching the full payload; we support partial caching and explicit cache keys.
[03:29] Ethan: about batching — we have realtime latency targets for routing (target p50 ~200ms). batching helps cost but hurts latency, how do you balance?
[03:38] Maya: exactly, that's the classic tradeoff — Redwood's autoscaler and continuous batching allow micro-batches that hit a sweet spot: small groups at low latency. you can set latency SLOs and configs that prioritize latency over batch size. dedicated gives more predictable throughput so you can run slightly larger batches without tail latency spikes.
[04:01] Priya: For the pilot we want to keep p95 under 400ms and average cost under $0.01 per call — does that seem feasible?
[04:09] Jordan: possibly. depends on model choice and completion length. if you go with a 7B quantized model on dedicated with a KV cache, achieving p95 350-400ms for 350-token completions is plausible. hosted could hit it too but the cost variance is wider.
[04:27] Priya: what about fallbacks — say dedicated capacity is saturated, do you have auto-fallback to hosted?
[04:33] Maya: yes. Redwood supports smart routing and policy-based fallback — you can route to hosted as overflow, or to cheaper model variants. that helps maintain availability but may change latency and cost.
[04:46] Ethan: security — SOC2, audit logs, RBAC? we need audit trails and KMS with customer-managed keys.
[04:54] Jordan: we support SOC2, provide audit logs, SAML/SSO, RBAC and KMS integrations. in private deployments you can bring your own HSM. we'll share the security pack after this call.
[05:05] Priya: good. do you keep customer data for training?
[05:08] Maya: no default training. hosted preserves request logs for debugging but we can disable retention or configure strict retention/PII rules. dedicated/private can be set to zero retention.
[05:19] Lina: about network egress — if we route to hosted, outbound traffic will go across our cloud egress link, which is metered. how much egress do you expect for a 2M token pilot?
[05:28] Jordan: token bytes are small relative to payloads, but embeddings and attachments increase egress. for pure text at 350 tokens average, egress is roughly a few GBs per month; we can produce a tighter estimate if you share exact payload sizes.
[05:44] Priya: ok. next on budget: you mentioned reserved capacity for dedicated — what commitment levels?
[05:50] Maya: we offer monthly and annual reserved pools. monthly reserved is for predictable traffic — lowest per-token comes with annual committed usage. for pilots we usually recommend a small monthly dedicated pool or run hosted pilot with a short dedicated spike to estimate.
[06:06] Ethan: and does dedicated require a private network peering? any additional infra ops?
[06:11] Jordan: dedicated can be configured with private peering (VPC peering) or via an IP allowlist and TLS. private deployment is the full VPC-controlled control plane. dedicated is between hosted and private in terms of ops.
[06:24] Priya: ok, let's talk pilot success criteria — what should we validate in two weeks?
[06:29] Maya: propose: 1) p95 latency < 400ms for 350-token completions on chosen model; 2) token unit cost under target (we'll model three configs hosted/dedicated/quantized); 3) KV caching effectiveness (measure cache hit rate and token reduction); 4) verify security controls (audit logs, KMS).
[06:48] Priya: that aligns. finance will sign off if we can show cost projections and a clean security review.
[06:53] Jordan: action item — we'll run a mock benchmark using your prompt set. can we get the prompts and any privacy redaction rules by end of week?
[06:59] Priya: yes, i'll get that to you.
[07:02] Lina: one more — are there cold start implications for the KV cache on first requests?
[07:07] Jordan: cold start is just the first few calls; cache warms quickly for repeated prefixes. we can preload common prefixes if you give us a list.
[07:17] Ethan: how about unit economics when you introduce multi-tenant vs single-tenant? if shared hosted is cheaper per token on small scale, but we need isolation for some flows.
[07:27] Maya: correct — shared hosted is cheapest initially. dedicated for reserved capacity gives predictability and lower variance; private is for compliance. we can model per-token equivalent costs for each runway.
[07:38] Priya: any immediate blockers on our side for a hosted pilot?
[07:41] Ethan: we need egress approval and our security review to allow outbound to Redwood API endpoints; that's a 1–2 day ops task.
[07:49] Priya: plus we need an internal PoC owner for the prompt set and evaluation metrics — i'll name someone after this call.
[07:56] Maya: great. I'll send the pricing spreadsheet and an initial pilot SOW. Jordan will send the benchmark plan and a small test harness.
[08:05] Jordan: i'll include the KV cache experiment and batching configs so we can measure cost/loss in latency tradeoffs.
[08:12] Priya: excellent. timeline — can we kick pilot the week of 9/6?
[08:16] Maya: yes, target start week of 9/6, benchmark on 9/8-9/10 and review 9/13.
[08:23] Lina: can you also share a rough per-token sensitivity table showing cost at different batch sizes / cache hit rates? that's helpful for our finance team.
[08:30] Jordan: yep — i'll include 3 scenarios (no cache/high latency target, moderate cache/mid latency target, high cache/dedicated).
[08:38] Priya: thanks, that should make it easier to compare.
[08:41] Maya: cool — any other questions?
[08:44] Ethan: nothing from me.
[08:46] Priya: nope. thanks both.
[08:48] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with the documents and schedule.

Recap / Next Steps (automated): send pricing, security pack, benchmark plan; customer to provide prompt set and PII rules; schedule technical deep-dive 2026-09-03 and pilot start week 2026-09-06.
